title: Gorgon Group
summary: The Gorgon Group is an activity cluster that public reporting, most prominently from Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 in 2018, describes as conducting both espionage style intrusion and ordinary criminal operations, which makes it a useful example of how motivation and tooling diverge. Reported victims included government bodies in the United Kingdom, Spain, Russia and the United States, alongside other sectors chosen for financial return. The delivery chain relied on documents using remote template injection, where the file itself contains little and fetches its real content from an attacker controlled address when opened, followed by publicly available remote access families and, in some campaigns, simple file encrypting ransomware deployed by the same operators. The group has also been reported hosting payloads on legitimate cloud infrastructure and using ordinary consumer services for staging and exfiltration. Because the same operators appear in both collection and extortion activity, and because their tools are widely shared, defenders should treat tool overlap as weak evidence of identity. Evidence worth collecting includes document process trees showing outbound web requests at open time, downloaded templates from cloud storage, remote access software installed outside change control, credential access attempts on workstations, and signs of file encryption or deletion of backup copies. The frequent misunderstanding is that a commodity tool implies a commodity adversary; here the tooling is commodity while the targeting and persistence are deliberate.

beginner.definition: The Gorgon Group is a name for attackers who do two different jobs. They spy on governments and also commit crimes for money. Public reports describe them since around 2016. They fetch extra content through documents and they use ransomware, which locks files until a payment is made.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers often borrow tools from crime, so the software alone does not tell you their goal. A document can look harmless at the door and collect its real contents later. This means your email filter must watch what a document does, not only what it contains. It also means ransomware and silent data theft often happen in the same incident.
howItWorks: The attacker sends a document that looks like a routine business or government file.
The document holds only a small instruction, not the harmful programme itself.
When the reader opens it, the document requests a page from an outside server.
That page returns the real content, often a macro that starts the harmful code.
The attacker then installs remote access software to control the computer quietly.
Data is copied out, and sometimes files are locked to demand a payment.
beginner.example: Think of a sealed envelope that contains only a note saying your parcel is waiting at a warehouse across town. The envelope passes every check at the gate because there is nothing dangerous inside it. The real delivery happens later, at a building nobody inspected, when you follow the instruction yourself. A document with a remote template works exactly like that note. The harmless part arrives first, and the harmful part arrives only after you have already trusted it.
takeaways: Some documents download their harmful part only after you open them, so behaviour matters.
You cannot judge the goal of an attacker from the tools that they use.
Store backups away from the main network and test that you can restore them.

objectives: Explain remote template injection and why the first stage of a document looks harmless.
Describe why attachment filtering must consider behaviour and not only file content.
Explain what ransomware does and why tested backups are the primary recovery control.
Identify the clues that an intrusion is financially motivated rather than espionage.
Explain why shared tooling weakens attribution and what evidence is stronger.
